articles.title: A food bank founded in Oklahoma in 1980 has distributed its billionth meal across 53 counties; at the November 10 milestone, the Oklahoma City Thunder donated $25,000, enough to provide another 75,000 meals
articles.summary: Reaching one billion meals is a remarkable milestone, but for a food bank serving families facing hunger, it also represents decades of work and a
articles.body: Reaching one billion meals is a remarkable milestone, but for a food bank serving families facing hunger, it also represents decades of work and a continuing need for support. The Regional Food Bank of Oklahoma has reached the landmark after 46 years of distributing food to communities across the state, relying on volunteers, donors, schools and local organisations to reach people who need assistance.In a November 12, 2026, press release published by Free Press Oklahoma City, the Regional Food Bank announced that it had packaged its one billionth meal during a ceremony held at its headquarters on November 10. The event brought together employees, community members, donors and partners. The Oklahoma City Thunder also marked the occasion with a surprise $25,000 donation through its Community Foundation, an amount the organisation said could provide another 75,000 meals.Food bank reaches billion-meal milestoneFounded in 1980, the Regional Food Bank of Oklahoma has spent 46 years working to address hunger across central and western Oklahoma. It distributes food through a network of community-based partner agencies and schools serving 53 counties. The billionth meal was prepared and celebrated at the organisation's headquarters in Oklahoma City before being sent to a neighbour in need. According to KOCO News, the milestone meal was loaded onto a truck during the ceremony as attendees celebrated the achievement.Stacy Dykstra, chief executive officer of the Regional Food Bank, said the milestone reflected the organisation's work and the support it had received since its establishment. She also described the achievement as a reminder of the difficult circumstances that bring Oklahoma families to food assistance providers. Dykstra emphasised that the organisation's progress would not have been possible without its partners, advocates, donors, volunteers, employees and board members.Oklahoma City Thunder contributes $25,000The celebration received additional support from the Oklahoma City Thunder, which presented the Regional Food Bank with a $25,000 donation through the Thunder Community Foundation. According to the food bank's press release, the contribution is equivalent to 75,000 meals for people experiencing food insecurity.Erin Oldfield, executive director of the Thunder Community Foundation, said the donation reflected the importance of working together to support families facing hunger. She highlighted that behind every meal is an individual, family or child dealing with circumstances that can make access to food difficult. The contribution also demonstrated the role that sports organisations and community partners can play in supporting local hunger-relief programmes.Food insecurity remains a major concernDespite reaching the billion-meal milestone, the Regional Food Bank said the need for assistance remains substantial. The organisation pointed to continuing economic pressures, including inflation and changes affecting access to federal food assistance. Its November 12 announcement also cited Feeding America's Map the Meal Gap report, which identified Oklahoma as having the second-highest overall food insecurity rate in the country and the highest rate of child food insecurity.The food bank works with community partners to ensure that food reaches children, older adults and working families who struggle to afford regular meals. Its distribution network includes schools and local agencies that understand the needs of the communities they serve. Dykstra said no single organisation could solve hunger independently. Continued cooperation between food banks, donors, volunteers and community organisations remains essential to reaching people across the state's 53 counties.Organisation looks towards its next milestoneThe Regional Food Bank said its work would continue beyond the billionth meal, with the long-term goal of ensuring that no Oklahoma resident goes hungry. Dykstra expressed confidence that the organisation would reach its next major milestone sooner, noting that it would not necessarily take another 46 years to distribute two billion meals.As the holiday season approaches, the food bank is encouraging people to contribute through donations, volunteering and community food drives. Its milestone marks decades of collective effort, but the organisation says continued public support will be necessary to address the needs of families who still struggle to put food on the table.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Texas family's 1921 bluebonnet painting was almost given to Goodwill during a move; relatives saved it, later identified it as a Julian Onderdonk original and sold it for $112,500 at auction in 2024
articles.summary: Sometimes a family heirloom that was forgotten turns out to be worth much more than anyone could have imagined.
articles.body: Sometimes a family heirloom that was forgotten turns out to be worth much more than anyone could have imagined. A 100-year-old painting of Texas bluebonnets that was almost thrown out with donations headed for Goodwill turned out to be a valuable piece of American art. A sentimental family heirloom turned out to be something of a surprise for its owners, who sold it at auction for $112,500, bringing new attention to the legacy of celebrated Texas painter Julian Onderdonk.Painting saved by last-minute decisionCBS News and The Washington Post reported that the painting was a gift to Carlotta Preston from a distant relative to mark her birth in 1922. The work, finished a year earlier, was kept by the family for decades, with no one identifying its artistic or monetary value.The painting was almost lost when the family moved from California to Washington state. When relatives helped Preston clear out her belongings in preparation for retirement, several items were loaded onto a trailer to be donated to Goodwill. One of them was the bluebonnet artwork. But Preston changed his mind at the last minute and kept it for its looks.After her death, the painting was hanging in the home of her daughter near Tacoma, Washington. It wasn’t until the family started researching the origins of the painting that they discovered it was an original by Julian Onderdonk, often described as the defining Texas landscape painter.Who was Julian Onderdonk?Julian Onderdonk was born in San Antonio in 1882 and showed an interest in art from an early age. He had artistic talent as a child and started teaching art as a teenager, according to CBS News.Later he relocated to New York City to pursue his artistic studies and teaching opportunities. His connection to Texas, however, remained strong.In 1906, Onderdonk took a seasonal job organizing art exhibits at the Dallas State Fair. Three years later he returned to Texas with his family and his painting began to take on the natural landscape of the state.Bluebonnets became a signature of his work. In spring, Texas is covered with these striking wildflowers and many of his most celebrated impressionist landscapes drew their inspiration from them.Family heirloom fetches six figures at auctionCBS News reports that the painting, A Field of Bluebonnets, San Antonio, was eventually consigned to Heritage Auctions in Dallas.On June 29, 2024, the artwork was sold for $112,500. The result placed the family heirloom among the more notable sales at an auction that featured other Onderdonk works. Another two of the artist's paintings sold for $106,250 and $93,750 respectively.Texas Monthly also chronicled the family’s efforts to get the valuable artwork home safely to Dallas. Preston's grandson, Jared Brinkley, flew in from Seattle with the century-old painting, which had been protected for the journey with foam, cardboard and packing materials.The find turned a simple decorative object into a work of art with historical importance, privately owned by the family for more than a century.A painting done toward the close of his lifeCBS News says that in 1921, a year before he died in 1922, Onderdonk painted A Field of Bluebonnets, San Antonio. He died at the height of his artistic success, his body of work inextricably linked to Texas identity and landscape.His paintings are still in major American art collections, such as the Amon Carter Museum of American Art in Fort Worth and the San Antonio Museum of Art.The Washington Post, in a feature article, noted the surprising financial return that the rediscovery of the artwork represented for the Brinkley family, and Texas Monthly documented the personal meaning of preserving and transporting such a rare family possession.The painting’s journey from possible Goodwill donation to six-figure auction sale is a perfect case study in how family heirlooms can carry unrecognized historical and artistic significance for generations. articles.title: A Chinese vase held open a Birmingham family’s door for 36 years; made during Emperor Qianlong’s reign, it stunned bidders by selling for £650,000
articles.summary: A Chinese vase, used as a doorstop by a Birmingham family for 36 years, stunned bidders by selling for £650,000 at Hansons Auctioneers, highlighting the vase's historical significance from the Qianlong period.
articles.body: A Chinese porcelain vase stood in a Birmingham family’s home for 36 years. It performed an ordinary household job, like holding a door open. The vase’s owners had inherited it from a great-aunt who had once worked as an antiques dealer. They, however, were not familiar with its full historical significance. The vase was even considered for sale at a local car boot sale before an antiques specialist examined it and recognised its importance, and on July 1, 2016, the object was sold at Hansons Auctioneers in Derbyshire for a hammer price of £650,000. This sale transformed the long-overlooked door holder into a major auction discovery.According to Hansons, the vase's journey into the family started decades earlier, with its story dating back to the 1920s when a great-aunt of the family acquired it in Cornwall. It was later inherited by the family in the 1980s, after which it remained in the household for years. The vase’s size, along with its weight, made it useful as a doorstop. Furthermore, it reportedly became the centre of childhood ball games.An imperial-period Chinese vase used in an ordinary hallwayThe object was a blue-and-white Chinese porcelain vase, which was around 66 centimetres tall, with a distinctive hexagonal outline. The decoration showcased branches bearing pomegranates and peaches, alternating with flowering branches. It was painted in different shades of cobalt blue. On its base, there was a Qianlong mark. The Qianlong Emperor ruled during the Qing dynasty from 1735 to 1796. His era name is commonly associated with the period 1736-1795. Auction specialists have listed the vase as from the Qianlong period, though a reign mark by itself cannot establish the age of the object.Charles Hanson, founder of Hansons Auctioneers, described the vase’s decorations as a combination of European Baroque design influences with a traditional Chinese heaped and piled effect that was associated with earlier Ming blue-and-white porcelain. A similarly designed vase can be found in the Nanjing Museum in China, while related examples are held in other museums and private collections. Such comparisons helped place the Birmingham object within a broader tradition of Chinese porcelain design.The auction house founder suggested that the vase might have been produced by imperial kilns for the Qianlong Emperor’s Summer Palace. Hansons’ Asian art consultant Adam Schoon, in a subsequent account, noted that the vase would have been made for one of the imperial palaces. Furthermore, its decoration was likely influenced by artists working on porcelain during the preceding Yongzheng period. It is worth noting that there are only assessments by specialists rather than documented records identifying the precise palace for which it was intended.From a home valuation to a £650,000 auction verdictThe vase’s rediscovery happened during a routine home visit by Hansons. In the hallway of a bungalow in the Midlands, Adam Schoon spotted the vase. The height and distinctive nature of the object prompted Schoon to have a better look. The Qianlong mark on the base added another detail for the specialists to investigate as they assessed its period and significance.Following the assessment, the auction house assigned the vase an estimate of £300,000 to £500,000. Collectors from China, Taiwan and Hong Kong reportedly expressed their interest, thus reflecting the international demand for important Chinese ceramics. The family decided to seek a professional valuation instead of selling the object casually. This decision became significant, as it had once nearly gone to a car boot sale.On July 1, 2016, the vase went under the hammer in Derbyshire. Exceeding the upper end of its estimate, the vase achieved £650,000. The result was reported by ITV News and Hansons as a record hammer price for the auction house’s sale at the time.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A CCTV footage from a clothing showroom in West Delhi's Moti Nagar has captured the final moments of an 18-year-old girl, showing her

Her body was found inside the trial room by the staff later that evening, police said.According to the preliminary investigation, Shabnam and Suraj were on friendly terms, but their relationship had reportedly turned sour over the past few months. The woman then reached the showroom.Some people examined the CCTV footage and noticed that the man had left the premises, but Shabnam had not."Suspecting that she could still be inside, they returned to the showroom around 8.30pm and began searching the premises. During the search, they noticed her scarf lying near the trial room. They also spotted blood seeping out from underneath the door," the officer said.Her body was found around 9pm, following which the police were called.A police team that reached the spot found injury marks on her neck caused by a sharp-edged weapon, along with a blood-stained knife near her body. articles.title: While digging a 24-foot North Dakota water well in 1920, Henry Stahl saw horses reject oily water; the land drew an $8,000 offer and a $10,000 valuation
articles.summary: In 1920, Henry Stahl's quest for water led to an astonishing oil discovery in North Dakota, transforming his property value and sparking local interest.
articles.body: For Henry Stahl of North Dakota, a routine effort to find drinking water for his horses in 1920 turned into a chance observation. According to the Prairie Public Dakota Datebook, Stahl was drilling a well near his farm in Williston. When the black sand began to show up in his drills, Stahl knew he was hitting oil. The water was probably contaminated with it, as the horses refused to drink from the pump Stahl had installed. But soon the news got out to local businessmen, the curious, and potential buyers. Stahl's property, worth $500 prior to the 1920s, had an $8,000 offer in cash and was then estimated to be worth $10,000.An ordinary water well revealed something unusual For several weeks, Stahl dug a well near his house, reaching a depth of 24 feet. His aim was simply to secure an accessible water supply. When he struck water on April 17, 1920, he also encountered approximately 14 inches of black sand that resembled oil-bearing material. After installing a pump, he offered the water to his horses, but they refused to drink it. Looking more closely, he noticed a thick film of oil floating on the water's surface. Curious about the discovery, Stahl continued testing the well. He pumped it dry and allowed it to refill, repeatedly finding between a quarter of at least two inches of light-coloured oil floating on top.Local interest grew as the oil attracted attentionNews of the find travelled rapidly among the towns' entrepreneurs. Pioneer Oil and Gas had already acquired tens of thousands of acres around the site and was believed to be drilling in the region for oil only a mile from Stahl's land. He suspected that the region's underground oil layer probably stretched under his property as well, and after gathering samples of water, he brought them to town. A few local entrepreneurs thought the water was potentially valuable and came to the well to examine it themselves.Following the news, there was a great interest in the public as well. Based on the newspaper report of that time, as referred to by Prairie Public, many people journeyed to the property in hopes of getting some of the oil. As more and more attention was given to the discovery, the value of the land increased from the original value of $500. One visitor offered him $ 8,000 in cash, which he refused. Then the land was finally valued at $10,000.North Dakota's commercial oil discovery came decades laterWhile such finds are exciting, we must separate the impact of an oil-producing water well from the existence of a producing underground reservoir. Confirming oil in the shallow aquifer does not suggest that the property held economically recoverable reserves. Subsequent petroleum geology research in the region went a long way toward explaining the basin's overall capacity. A Mountain Geologist examined the Bakken formation and identified it as both a source of oil and a reservoir for continuous petroleum accumulation across parts of North Dakota and Montana.North Dakota's first commercial oil find came several decades later. The Clarence Iverson No. 1 well, located near Tioga, began producing oil on April 4, 1951, marking the beginning of North Dakota's commercial oil industry. The discovery came after years of exploration and geologic studies. Stahl's farm experience in 1920 was, therefore, a brief episode in North Dakota Petroleum history. What started as a farmer with horses refusing to drink from a new well turned into a local curiosity, then into unsolicited offers for his farm, and finally into a focus on oil resources in western North Dakota.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Highly destructive and political decision’: Trump slams judge’s order blocking Washington golf course renovation
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has vowed to challenge a federal judge's order delaying work on a historic public golf course in Washington, calling the ruling
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has vowed to challenge a federal judge's order delaying work on a historic public golf course in Washington, calling the ruling a “highly destructive and political decision”.Trump said on Sunday that his administration would immediately appeal the temporary restraining order issued by US District Judge Ana Reyes, which temporarily blocks the planned closure of the golf course for 15 months and delays the renovation work until at least November 28.According to the Associated Press (AP), the order came just hours before the course was due to shut on Sunday for redevelopment. Trump wants to transform the public facility along the Potomac River into a championship-level golf venue.In a post on his social media platform, Trump criticised the condition of the course, saying it was in a “terrible state of disrepair”. Sharing photographs of the site, he added: “They don’t call it Trash Island for no reason!”The redevelopment plan has been challenged by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers, who filed a lawsuit in February. They argue that the project would change the character of the publicly accessible course and make it unaffordable for many visitors. Trump has denied those claims.Judge Reyes issued the temporary restraining order on Saturday after considering Trump's social media posts announcing that the park would close on November 15 for the renovation. She said the posts indicated that the redevelopment plan was final and that the National Park Service would shut the park to carry it out.The judge said both factors supported granting the plaintiffs' request for another temporary restraining order. The order prevents the government from closing East Potomac Park and the golf course during their usual public hours and remains in effect until November 28, or until the court issues another direction.The Justice Department said the ruling did not prevent the administration from continuing to plan the redevelopment. It added that the National Park Service could still restrict access to facilities where public safety was at risk.The case is among several legal challenges to Trump's plans to reshape parts of the US capital. Other projects include a proposed memorial arch and a White House ballroom. A separate judge recently delayed work on the arch for 14 days.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Rare bar-headed goose, that flies over the Himalayas, spotted at Nandur Madhmeshwar after nearly a decade
articles.summary: Rare bar-headed goose spotted at Nandur Madhmeshwar Wildlife Sanctuary after 8–10 years, signaling wetland revival and success of habitat restoration efforts.
articles.body: Nashik: A bird that routinely does what few creatures on Earth can has returned to Nashik after nearly a decade.The bar-headed goose, famed for flying over the Himalayas and surviving at altitudes where oxygen levels are dangerously low, has been spotted at Nandur Madhmeshwar Wildlife Sanctuary after a gap of eight to 10 years. Forest officials say its return is more than a rare sighting. It is a sign that conservation efforts at Maharashtra’s premier wetland sanctuary are beginning to pay off.The arrival of the bird, along with several other uncommon migratory species, comes after nearly 18 months of focused habitat and water management interventions at the sanctuary. Wildlife officials believe the improved conditions have helped restore Nandur Madhmeshwar’s status as an important stopover on one of Asia’s major migratory routes.“The bar-headed goose breeds in the extreme high-altitude regions of Tibet and China. As severe winter snowfall sets in, these birds undertake an arduous migration along the Central Asian and East Asian Flyway toward Northeast and South India,” said range forest officer Hiralal Chaudhari.The significance of the sighting lies not only in the bird’s rarity but also in what it represents. Often described as the world’s highest-flying bird, the bar-headed goose is known for crossing the Himalayas, including the Mount Everest region, during migration, enduring sub-zero temperatures and extremely thin air that would challenge most wildlife species.“Unlike most birds, this species flies directly over Mount Everest in harsh weather conditions characterized by sub-zero temperatures and severely low oxygen levels,” Chaudhari said.For conservationists, the return of such a species is a strong indicator of habitat quality. Migratory birds are highly sensitive to changes in water levels, food availability and human disturbance. Their presence often reflects the ecological health of wetlands.“Nandur Madhmeshwar serves as a vital stopover on this Asian Flyway where favorable conditions have prompted them to extend their stay. Krushna Bhawar, the deputy conservator of forests (wild life) took a keen interest in the works undertaken here and it has resulted in some species visiting the site after 8 to 14 years of gap,” Chaudhari added.The sanctuary, often called the “Bharatpur of Maharashtra”, currently supports more than 310 recorded bird species, including over 140 migratory species. Officials point to other encouraging signs as well. A white stork was recently recorded after a gap of 14 years, revealing the impact of recent restoration measures.Every winter, thousands of birds arrive from Central Asia, Siberia, China and other northern regions to escape freezing temperatures. Their journeys span thousands of kilometres, making safe stopovers such as Nandur Madhmeshwar critical to their survival.Comparing the annual congregation to Nashik’s biggest religious gathering, Chaudhari said, “The sanctuary is witnessing its own avian Kumbh Mela.”You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Nashik | Silver Rate in Nashik | Bank Holidays in Nashik | Public Holidays in Nashik | Petrol Price in Nashik | Diesel Price in Nashik | CNG Price in Nashik | LPG Price in NashikStay updated with the latest Nashik news. articles.title: Siri AI on Mac: How to enable it in macOS 27 Golden Gate, supported models, and what's new
articles.summary: Siri on the Mac has always been the version people forget is there, tucked into a menu bar icon most users click once and never again.
articles.body: Siri on the Mac has always been the version people forget is there, tucked into a menu bar icon most users click once and never again. The rebuilt assistant that arrived with macOS 27 Golden Gate on September 14 goes after that problem from a different angle, by putting itself inside Spotlight, inside the Control-click menu and behind a screenshot shortcut. The fastest way to reach Siri AI on a desktop now involves no talking at all.Mac owners also got a break nobody else did. Apple has withheld Siri AI from iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch across the European Union, yet Macs are carved out of that restriction. An EU account on macOS 27 Golden Gate can run the assistant provided the system language and Siri language are both English. Accounts registered in mainland China remain locked out on every device Apple sells.How to turn on Siri AI on your MacSwitching it on is quick, but finishing the setup does not mean you can use it yet:Install macOS 27 Golden GateOpen System Settings and select SiriClick Try Siri AI (Beta), or Turn On Siri first if Siri is disabledChoose a voice, complete voice enrollment, then work through the privacy screenThe last of those puts you on a waitlist and the download begins on its own once you clear it. Apple gives no estimate for the wait, and reports since launch have swung between a few minutes and most of an afternoon. Running Apple Intelligence before you upgraded buys you nothing here, because that earlier consent does not carry over.Which Macs support Siri AITwo lines cover eligibility. The A18 Pro MacBook Neo qualifies, and so does any Mac running M1 or newer. Intel machines are out, with no beta workaround.Underneath that sits a narrower requirement most people miss. Expressive voices, the setting that lets you dial Siri's pace and expressiveness, needs AFM Core Advanced, Apple's newest on-device model. On the Mac that translates to an M3 chip or later with at least 12GB of unified memory. An M1 MacBook Air will run the assistant fine and never see those controls.Language is the other limit. English is all Siri AI speaks for now, with French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish due next month, and both your system language and Siri language have to match a supported option.What Siri AI can do on macOSMost of the Mac-specific engineering has gone into access points rather than fresh abilities:Spotlight: the assistant is built in, so open-ended questions go into the same field you use to launch appsContext menus: Control-click an image, a file or a passage of text to ask about it without leaving what you are doingVisual Intelligence: a keyboard shortcut captures what is on your display, a PDF included, then lets you search it or type a question about itWrite with Siri: draft from nothing, revise what exists, or ask for notes on it, almost anywhere you type. Mail and Messages pick up the punctuation and tone you normally use with each recipientSystemwide proofreading: grammar and spelling are checked as you type, inside most third-party apps as well as Apple's ownPersonal context: questions about your own mail, messages, calendar and notes are answered from those sourcesThe Siri app: iCloud carries conversation history across devices, so something started on an iPhone continues on the desktopDriving all of this is a new generation of Apple Foundation Models that the company says was built with Google, using its Gemini models. Requests are split between the Mac and Private Cloud Compute, where Apple's stated position is that personal data is never retained and stays out of reach of its own staff.Apple Intelligence features beyond Siri AIPhotos adds Spatial Reframing, an Extend tool and a rebuilt Clean Up. Image Playground handles photorealistic output now and accepts edits by description, with SynthID watermarking due in a later release. Safari sorts tabs into topics by itself, tracks pages for restocks or price cuts through Notify Me, and assembles custom extensions from a written brief. Shortcuts takes the same route to automations, and Calendar accepts plain-language changes to events.Siri AI usage limits and what Apple plans to chargeAnything routed through Apple's servers, Siri AI included, draws on a daily allowance. The company has declined to publish a number, saying the ceiling moves with the feature, the complexity of the request and how loaded the system is at the time.What Apple has committed to is charging for expanded access at some point. There is no price, no date, and no indication of whether the current free allowance survives once that tier exists.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? articles.summary: Iran ramped up strikes in Bahrain early Sunday morning, carrying out a six-drone attack on a U.S. airbase. Bahrain said it had intercepted “several aerial attacks” before they hit their targets. Iran, meanwhile, claimed it had struck a base. articles.body:
Iran ramped up strikes in Bahrain early Sunday morning, carrying out a six-drone attack on a U.S. airbase.

Bahrain said it had intercepted “several aerial attacks” before they hit their targets. Iran, meanwhile, claimed it had struck a base .

This comes two days after Iran reported it had attacked a U.S. early-warning radar facility also in Bahrain, but the U.S. military denied it, saying it had intercepted the drones without damage.

The Gulf kingdom had not been struck by Iran since a blitz in September. U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao at the time said that the Iranian military “blew the hell” out of it.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said that Sunday’s strikes were in retaliation for “hostile US actions,” Iran’s Fars News Agency reported.

Esmail Baghaei, a spokesperson for the Iranian Foreign Ministry, said at a press conference Sunday that the country would continue to respond to military aggression by the U.S. and other countries.

The U.S. continues to maintain a naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz as the war pushes past the eight-month mark.

It has also continued to carry out limited defensive strikes. Earlier this month, U.S. warplanes struck an anti-aircraft site on Qeshm Island and another island in the Strait of Hormuz.

Diplomatic attempts to end the conflict have stalled. President Trump earlier this week called the war “ effectively over ” and “won” by the U.S. He also said he was unlikely to order fresh attacks as long as talks to end the war continue positively.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Wednesday accused the U.S. of threatening to attack his country with America’s “mother of all bombs,” its largest non-nuclear weapon, even as the U.S. pursues a peace deal.

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt condemned Iran’s Sunday attacks in solidarity with Bahrain.

articles.title: A San Francisco couple bought a neglected Victorian for $1.85 million in 2022, rebuilt its interiors and added a separate apartment; the restored 'Painted Lady' is now asking $5.595 million
articles.summary: A neglected Queen Anne Victorian in San Francisco’s Noe Valley has returned to market with a $5.595 million asking price after a couple bought it for
articles.body: A neglected Queen Anne Victorian in San Francisco’s Noe Valley has returned to market with a $5.595 million asking price after a couple bought it for $1.85 million in 2022 and rebuilt much of the home from the studs. The restoration, reported by Mansion Global and detailed in the Sotheby’s International Realty listing, turned the century-old property at 551 Alvarado Street into a five-bedroom residence with a separate one-bedroom apartment, while preserving the colourful character that gives it its “Painted Lady” identity.The project is a reminder that restoring an older home is often about far more than fresh paint and new furniture. Behind the cheerful facade, the owners replaced the foundation, added structural steel, rebuilt framing, upgraded electrical service, and reworked plumbing, heating, cooling, roofing, and drainage systems.A Victorian with historyThe house dates to 1900 and sits in Noe Valley, one of San Francisco’s sought-after residential neighbourhoods. Its Queen Anne-style facade includes a classic three-sided bay window, a recessed portico, and decorative frieze bands, features that give the property its period presence even after extensive modern work.The term “Painted Ladies” is often associated with San Francisco’s famous rows of colourful Victorians, but it also refers more broadly to the three-colour paint style used on Victorian houses across the city. This home embraces that tradition with a bright coral exterior that makes it stand out on its block.When Randy LaRoche and David Laudon purchased the property in 2022, it had already been altered considerably over the years. The couple, both members of the Victorian Alliance of San Francisco, saw an opportunity to bring the home back to life rather than simply modernise its interior.A full rebuild, not a refreshLaRoche, a third-generation San Franciscan who has restored four other Victorians, and his husband, Laudon, reset the entire layout of the house. They installed new kitchens and bathrooms and added a garage, a change that was approved despite some pushback from a neighbour on the otherwise friendly street.The work went well beyond cosmetic upgrades. According to the listing, the home received a new foundation, structural steel, new framing, a 400-amp electrical service, completely reworked plumbing and heating and cooling systems, new windows and doors, six skylights, extensive insulation, and new roofing and drainage systems.That level of intervention explains why the listing describes the house as “almost entirely new” behind its historic exterior. The restoration was designed to preserve the character of a 1900 Victorian while making the building suitable for contemporary living.What buyers get nowThe restored home offers five bedrooms across 4,054 square feet, according to Mansion Global. It is arranged as a four-bedroom main residence with four and a half bathrooms, plus a separate two-level, one-bedroom apartment.The apartment can be used in several ways, whether for guests, staff, extended family, or as an independent living space. That flexibility is increasingly valuable in San Francisco, where multigenerational living, rental income, and separate workspaces have become practical considerations for many homeowners.Inside, the home features quarter-sawn American white oak floors, custom European-style cabinetry, detailed millwork, richly veined quartzite, and carefully selected stone and tile. The materials are intended to create warmth and texture while complementing the home’s Victorian bones.The price has changedSotheby’s International Realty agent Christopher Meza initially listed the property at $5.995 million. The asking price was later reduced to $5.595 million, a cut of $400,000, according to Mansion Global.Other listing platforms have shown slightly different figures at different times, including $5.695 million, reflecting updates to the public listing. The most recent reporting from Mansion Global puts the current ask at $5.595 million.The original purchase price of $1.85 million was recorded in July 2022. At that time, the property was described as a four-bedroom, two-bathroom Victorian with high ceilings, period detailing, pocket doors, a full-length attic space, and a sub-basement with storage.Why the project stands outThe jump from a $1.85 million purchase to a $5.595 million asking price reflects both the scale of the renovation and the value of the finished product. The owners did not merely update finishes, they rebuilt major systems and reconfigured the home to meet modern expectations.At the same time, the project shows the challenge of restoring older homes in a city like San Francisco. Historic character, neighbourhood context, planning approvals, structural needs, and modern conveniences all have to be balanced. The addition of a garage, for example, required approval despite objections from at least one neighbour.The result is a home that looks like a classic San Francisco Victorian from the street but functions like a newly built residence inside. That combination is exactly what the sellers hope will justify the asking price.A home with a storyFor buyers, 551 Alvarado Street offers more than square footage and bedrooms.
